title: Rhythm and repetition — Image Wiki
text:
Rhythm and repetition
  Repeating something turns many things into one thing — and the moment it does, whatever does not belong to the set becomes impossible to miss.

  
    Termrhythm and repetition
    Also calledrepetition, visual rhythm, motif, cadence
    Not the same aspattern as a surface property, gestalt similarity, symmetry
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensThe intervals do the talkingWhere it goes wrongAcross different mediaCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Find a building with a long row of identical windows. You will not count them. Your eye takes the row as a single thing — "the windows" — and moves on. Now one of them has its blind down. You find that one from across the street, immediately, without having gone looking for it.
That is this whole article in one observation. Repetition turns many things into one thing. And the instant it does, anything that does not belong to the set has nowhere to hide. Repeat something and you get unity; you also get, free of charge, the strongest emphasis available anywhere in composition.
Rhythm is the same repetition with the gaps counted. Getty's list of design principles carries pattern and rhythm side by side, and that is the right pairing: they are one mechanism read at two levels — what repeats, and how far apart (SRC-002).
Why it happens
Grouping runs before you get an opinion: things that resemble each other get filed together, and so do things that sit close together. Gestalt grouping covers that machinery, and proximity is one of the strongest cues in it (SRC-036). What matters here is the consequence, which is rarely spelled out.
Once a group has formed, the group is the thing you perceive, and its members stop being inspected. Fifty arches are one arcade. Two hundred tiles are one floor. Your eye samples the set, decides it has understood it, and spends its attention elsewhere.
A group also has an edge. Everything inside inherits the group's identity; everything outside is left standing alone. So the exception costs you nothing. You do not have to make the odd one bigger, brighter or redder — it is already the loudest object in the frame, purely because everything around it agreed on something and it did not. That is emphasis by exception, and it is cheap. Getty's definition of emphasis is exactly this move seen from the other side — one area is made to stand out by contrasting it with the others (SRC-002) — and repetition is the most efficient way to build the "others". Emphasis by shouting is expensive, and it has to out-shout everything else that shouts.



Prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, begun 785. Photograph by James (Jim) Gordon via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Count the ways this picture repeats: one column type, one arch shape, one red-and-white voussoir stripe, one spacing, repeated in two directions until it runs out of building. Nothing here is the subject, and nothing needs to be — the repetition itself is what you are looking at, and it produces total unity out of several hundred separate stones.
Now find the people. There is a child in a pale top walking between columns in the left third, and two seated visitors by the far wall on the right, next to a thin vertical slit of daylight. Each of them is small, low-contrast and easy to miss in a verbal description — and each of them is the first thing your eye lands on once you know they exist. They are the only objects in the frame that are not members of the set.
This also shows the cost. Look for thirty seconds and the arches stop registering. There is no interval anywhere that differs from any other, so after the third bay there is nothing left to find out, and the eye disengages.


The intervals do the talking

Regularevery gap the samereads as order, structure, machineryAcceleratingeach gap a quarter wider than the lastreads as movement, speed, recessionthe accentBrokenevery gap the same but one, which is doubledthe gap is the accent — nothing was added

Eight identical marks in all three panels, spanning the same width. The only thing that changes is the spacing.
Regular reads as order, measurement, machinery — sleepers, pylons, stitches, a barcode. Accelerating reads as movement, because gaps that shrink or grow are what perspective does to a row of equal things, and your eye has spent a lifetime reading shrinking intervals as "going away".
Broken is the one worth remembering. Nothing was added to that panel and nothing was made bigger. One gap is twice the others, and that gap is now the accent — the emphasis is in the space, not in an object.


Intervals that wander rather than change steadily read as organic: rain, footprints in snow, gulls on a beach. And rhythms nest. A brick wall has one cadence at the scale of a brick, another at the scale of a course, a third at the scale of a window opening, and all three sit in the same square metre. When a picture feels considered and you cannot say why, a nested rhythm is often what you are answering to.



Utagawa Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake, from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1857 (Library of Congress). Public domain.
Two rhythms doing opposite jobs in one print. The rain is one repeated mark — a long straight line — printed as two overlapping sets at slightly different angles, with uneven gaps. Nothing about it is measured, and that is why it reads as weather rather than as hatching: irregular intervals feel alive.
Under the bridge, the trestle is the other kind. Vertical posts at an even spacing, each with the same diagonal brace, repeated until the frame cuts it off — measured, still, structural.
Then the five people. They are the exception in a frame where almost everything is a member of some set, and they are what you look at, even though they are small, dark and low in contrast against the pale deck. The lone raftsman out on the water gets the same treatment: he is the only mark in an empty band.





The Pont du Gard, Roman aqueduct near Vers-Pont-du-Gard, first century CE. Photograph by Benh Lieu Song via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
Three tiers, three cadences, one arch shape. The top arcade repeats at a spacing so short and so even that you give up counting arches after four or five and read the whole thing as a band — it has crossed over from being a row of objects into being a surface. That crossing is the subject of Shape, texture and pattern.
The tall middle arcade does the opposite. Its arches are large and deliberately unequal: the widest one straddles the river channel, and they narrow as they go left across the gorge. So the point where the bridge crosses the water is marked by an interval rather than by an ornament — nothing was added there, one gap is simply bigger.


One caution before the failure modes. All of this is about how strongly things group, not about how loud they are. A repeated element and a high-contrast element pull in different currencies, and the two are easy to mistake for each other; see Contrast.
Where it goes wrong
Wallpaper. Repetition with no variation and no exception stops being read. It becomes a field the eye skims, and then it does not matter how much work went into it. The fix is not more repetition; it is one break.
A texture that swallows its own subject. Drawabox is blunt: draw every scale on the fish explicitly and you get visual noise — light and dark marks packed so densely that the eye shoots there and will not leave, whether or not that is where the subject is (SRC-078). Photography Life makes the same point from the other end: repeated elements give a photograph a reason to exist, and too much texture in unimportant areas only makes the frame look complicated (SRC-017, SRC-021).
A rhythm nobody chose. A row of five where the middle one is slightly out of step does not read as rhythm; it reads as a mistake, because your eye finds the exception, inspects it, and discovers nothing there.
Across different media

Painting and print. Islamic tilework, textile design and woodblock printing build whole surfaces out of one motif; a woodcut can repeat a mark thousands of times because the block does the work.
Photography. Repetition is usually found rather than made, which is why photographers wait: the fifth wave, the sixth pigeon, the bird that comes round again (SRC-021).
Design and posters. Cooper Hewitt's taxonomy of poster moves includes make a system — one family of colours and forms, applied across many pieces so that uniformity and variation both become available — and, as a deliberate opposite, overwhelm the eye, where dense repeated pattern is the point (POST-001-SUP1).

Common mistakes

"Repetition is decoration." It is the cheapest structural tool there is. It creates a group, and groups are what Visual hierarchy operates on.
"To emphasise something, make it stand out more." Often it is easier to make everything else agree. The exception does not need to be loud, only different.
"A pattern makes any picture stronger." A pattern with nothing to interrupt it makes a surface, not a picture.
"Rhythm means regular." Regular is one setting. Changing intervals and broken intervals are the interesting ones, and both are still rhythm.
"Identical is safest." Near-identical is the risky case. Truly identical elements group cleanly; almost-identical ones attract inspection they cannot repay.


Reading rhythm in an image

Name the thing that repeats. If nothing does, this article does not apply.
Squint and ask whether the repeats have merged into one mass. If they have, they are a surface, not a row of objects.
Measure the gaps by eye. Equal, steadily changing, or irregular?
Find the exception — the one element that is not a member of the set. Is it where the subject is?
If there is no exception anywhere, ask whether the frame has anything left for the eye to find on a second pass.
